---
title: "Regression models"
---

Suppose lexical decision latencies tend to decrease as word frequency increases. Before choosing a regression, we need to ask a more particular question: which feature of the response distribution should change with frequency, and what comparison would that change represent? A regression model answers these questions by allowing one or more parameters of a response distribution to depend on predictors. The response distribution states which measurements are possible and how they vary; the regression function states how its parameters change across declared predictor values.

This module assumes the earlier distinction among an [estimand, an estimator, and an estimate](../statistical-inference/properties-of-estimators.qmd#keeping-three-objects-distinct), along with the idea that a [likelihood holds the observed data fixed](../statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd#holding-the-data-fixed). We will point back to those objects when they do explanatory work. We will not rederive them under every regression.

We proceed in three passes. First, we build an ordinary linear regression slowly: [conditional means](regression-models.qmd) state the target, [simple linear regression](simple-linear-regression.qmd) restricts that mean to a line, and the fitting, uncertainty, residual, and diagnostic pages ask what the restriction licenses. This order keeps the linguistic comparison separate from the algorithm used to estimate it.

Once the one-predictor model is explicit, we add [multiple predictors](multiple-regression.qmd), [categorical predictors](coding-categorical-predictors.qmd), and [interactions](interactions.qmd). Each coefficient is interpreted as a comparison between conditional means under the coding and predictor values used in the model. Correlated-predictor and regularization pages then ask whether the observed design actually supplies that comparison.

## Other response distributions

A straight-line mean with normally distributed residuals is not appropriate for every linguistic response. Binary choices, ordinal judgments, counts, and bounded slider responses have different supports and patterns of variation. [Generalized linear models](why-generalized-linear-models.qmd) retain a predictor-dependent mean while changing the response distribution and the function relating that mean to a linear predictor.

Second, the generalized linear model pages treat binary responses, ordinal responses, counts, overdispersed counts, and bounded responses separately. The distribution is chosen from the observation process, not from the shape of the histogram alone. An elicited choice is not a grammaticality label, an ordinal annotation is not an interval measurement, and a corpus count does not become a rate until its opportunities have been represented.

## Repeated units

Third, linguistic datasets commonly contain repeated speakers, items, verbs, documents, or languages. The [structured-data page](structured-data.qmd) begins by identifying the response, sampling, and generalization units. Random intercepts represent persistent modeled differences among groups, while random slopes represent group variation in a predictor association. Mixed-effects models combine these terms with the response distributions introduced earlier.

The [chapter dependency graph](../learning-path.qmd) displays the linear, generalized-linear, and mixed-effects branches. If you are reading in order, begin with [conditional means](regression-models.qmd). If you arrived with a fitted model, begin instead by naming its response, its conditional target, and its repeated units; those three answers determine which branch you need.
